front: What is a p-value and what does it not tell you?
back: • p-value — probability of observing data at least as extreme as yours, assuming the null is true. • Does NOT tell you — probability that the null is true, probability that the alternative is true, effect size, practical significance. • p < 0.05 is a convention, not a law. • Common trap — p-value depends on sample size — large n makes tiny effects significant.

front: What is statistical power and what factors increase it?
back: • Power = P(reject null. • null is false) = 1 − β. • Increases with — larger sample size, larger true effect size, lower σ (noise), higher α. • Low power → high false negative rate — you miss real effects. • Underpowered studies — common in analytics — too small n to detect meaningful MDE. • Power is set before the experiment, not computed after.

front: What is the Central Limit Theorem and when does it fail?
back: • CLT — sum (or mean) of n independent, identically distributed RVs → normally distributed as n → ∞. • Enables use of z-tests and t-tests on non-normal data with large n. • Fails when — data is heavy-tailed (variance infinite), data is not independent, n is small and distribution is very skewed. • Practical rule — n ≥ 30 for reasonable approximation for many distributions.

front: What is the difference between confidence interval and credible interval?
back: • CI (frequentist) — if you repeated the experiment many times, 95% of constructed intervals would contain the true parameter — says nothing about this specific interval. • Credible interval (Bayesian) — 95% probability that the parameter lies in this interval, given the data and prior. • Common trap — saying "there is 95% probability the true value is in this CI" — this is the Bayesian interpretation, not the frequentist one.

front: What is the Law of Large Numbers?
back: • LLN — as sample size grows, sample mean converges to population mean. • Weak LLN — convergence in probability. • Strong LLN — almost sure convergence. • Enables empirical estimation of expectations. • Common trap — does not apply with infinite-variance distributions (e.g., Cauchy).

front: What is Simpson's Paradox and what causes it?
back: • A trend present in all subgroups reverses when data is aggregated. • Caused by a confounding variable that affects both group membership and the outcome. • Classic example — drug appears harmful overall but helpful in every subgroup separately. • How to fix it — stratify by the confounder; do not aggregate without checking composition. • Always check whether subgroup proportions differ between groups being compared.

front: What is Bayes' theorem and what are its components?
back: • P(A. • B) = P(B. • A) × P(A) / P(B). • P(A) — prior — belief before evidence. • P(B. • A) — likelihood — probability of evidence given hypothesis. • P(A. • B) — posterior — updated belief after evidence. • P(B) — marginal likelihood / normalizing constant. • Used in spam filters, naive Bayes, Bayesian updating, medical diagnostics.

front: What is the difference between standard deviation and standard error?
back: • SD — measures spread of individual observations around the mean. • SE — measures uncertainty in the sample mean = SD / √n. • SE shrinks with more data; SD does not. • Common trap — reporting SE instead of SD makes precision look artificially high. • Use SE when discussing the mean estimate; use SD when describing the data distribution.

front: What is covariance vs correlation and when is correlation misleading?
back: • Covariance — measures joint variability of two variables — scale-dependent. • Correlation — standardized covariance, range [−1, 1] — scale-free. • Pearson correlation measures linear association only. • Misleading when — relationship is non-linear, outliers are present (one outlier can dominate), Anscombe's quartet. • Zero correlation does not imply independence (unless jointly normal).

front: What is a t-test and when should you use Welch's t-test?
back: • t-test — tests whether means of two groups differ significantly. • Student's t-test — assumes equal variance across groups. • Welch's t-test — does not assume equal variance — adjusts degrees of freedom. • Use Welch's by default — no penalty when variances are equal, but protects when they aren't. • Common trap — using Student's t-test when group variances differ → inflated Type I error.

front: What is the multiple comparisons problem and how is it corrected?
back: • Testing k hypotheses at α each → probability of ≥ 1 false positive = 1 − (1−α)^k. • At α=0.05, 20 tests → ~64% chance of a false positive. • Bonferroni correction — α_adjusted = α / k — conservative but simple. • Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR) — controls false discovery rate — less conservative, better for large k. • Common trap — choosing which tests to report based on results is a form of multiple testing.

front: What is a null hypothesis and what are its two possible outcomes?
back: • Null hypothesis (H₀) — default assumption — typically "no effect" or "no difference". • Outcomes — reject H₀ (evidence against null) or fail to reject H₀ (insufficient evidence). • Failing to reject ≠ accepting the null — absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence. • Common trap — saying "we proved there is no effect" after a non-significant result.

front: What is the difference between parametric and non-parametric statistical tests?
back: • Parametric — assume data follows a distribution (usually normal) — t-test, ANOVA, Pearson. • Non-parametric — no distributional assumption — Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon, Spearman. • Non-parametric tests use ranks rather than raw values. • Use non-parametric when — small sample, heavy tails, ordinal data, distributional assumptions violated. • Tradeoff — non-parametric tests have lower power when parametric assumptions are actually met.

front: What is the expected value and how does linearity of expectation work?
back: • E[X] — weighted average of all possible values — sum(x × P(x)). • Linearity — E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y] — holds even if X and Y are dependent. • Useful for computing expectations of complex sums without knowing joint distribution. • Applies to — random algorithms, hashing, estimation problems.

front: What is a z-score and how is it used for anomaly detection?
back: • z-score = (x − μ) / σ — number of standard deviations from the mean. • . • z. • > 2 — ~5% of data under normality. • . • z. • > 3 — ~0.3% of data — common anomaly threshold. • Trap on seasonal data — comparing to wrong baseline inflates false positives. • How to fix it — compute z-score within day-of-week cohort or rolling window.

front: What is variance and why is E[X²] ≠ (E[X])²?
back: • Variance = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − (E[X])². • The gap between E[X²] and (E[X])² measures how spread out X is. • Var(X) = 0 iff X is a constant. • Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X) — shifting does not change variance, scaling does. • Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2Cov(X,Y).

front: What is a heavy-tailed distribution and why does it matter?
back: • Heavy-tailed — probability of extreme values decays slower than exponential. • Examples — Pareto, log-normal, power law. • Sample mean has high variance — CLT converges slowly or not at all (infinite-variance case). • Common in — revenue, social network connections, internet traffic. • Common trap — applying normal-distribution tools to heavy-tailed data underestimates tail risk.

front: What is the difference between MLE and method of moments?
back: • MLE — choose parameters that maximize likelihood of observed data. • Method of moments — set theoretical moments equal to sample moments and solve. • MLE is asymptotically efficient (achieves Cramér-Rao lower bound) — preferred when n is large. • Method of moments — simpler to compute, less efficient. • For some distributions (e.g., beta, gamma), both give closed-form solutions.

front: What is a sufficient statistic?
back: • A statistic T(X) is sufficient for θ if P(X. • T(X)) does not depend on θ. • Contains all information in the data about the parameter — no information lost by reducing to T. • Example — sample mean is sufficient for μ in a normal distribution with known σ. • Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem: formal condition for sufficiency. • Used to justify why summary statistics capture everything needed for inference.

front: What is overfitting in a statistical model vs a machine learning model?
back: • Both — model fits noise in training data — high in-sample fit, poor out-of-sample performance. • Statistical framing — model has too many parameters relative to sample size. • ML framing — model has too high capacity relative to data complexity. • Detection — large train-test gap; validation curve peaks then degrades. • Fix (stats) — fewer parameters, regularization, cross-validation, information criteria (AIC, BIC).

front: What is AIC and BIC and when does each favor simpler models?
back: • AIC = 2k − 2ln(L̂) — penalizes model complexity, selects model that balances fit and parsimony. • BIC = k×ln(n) − 2ln(L̂) — stronger penalty as n grows. • BIC selects simpler models than AIC when n is large. • Use AIC when — prediction is the goal; use BIC when: identifying the true model is the goal. • Both reward fit and penalize parameters — minimize to select.

front: What is the difference between frequentist and Bayesian inference philosophically?
back: • Frequentist — probability = long-run frequency of events; parameters are fixed, unknown constants. • Bayesian — probability = degree of belief; parameters have distributions; prior + likelihood → posterior. • Frequentist — can't assign probability to a single hypothesis being true. • Bayesian — naturally handles small samples, sequential updating, and prior knowledge. • Both are valid frameworks with different assumptions and outputs.

front: What is the law of total expectation?
back: • E[X] = E[E[X. • Y]] — the expectation of X equals the expectation of its conditional expectation given Y. • Useful for — computing expectations by conditioning on a simpler RV. • Example — E[revenue] = E[E[revenue. • user_segment]] — compute per segment then average. • Also known as the tower property or law of iterated expectations.

front: What is heteroscedasticity and why does it violate OLS assumptions?
back: • Heteroscedasticity — variance of residuals is not constant across observations. • OLS assumes homoscedasticity (constant variance). • Effect — OLS estimates remain unbiased but standard errors are wrong — hypothesis tests invalid. • Detection — plot residuals vs fitted values; Breusch-Pagan test. • How to fix it — robust standard errors (HC estimators) or transform the outcome variable.

front: What is a bootstrap and when is it useful?
back: • Bootstrap — repeatedly resample (with replacement) from data, compute statistic each time, use distribution for inference. • Useful when — analytical distribution of statistic is unknown, sample is small. • Provides empirical SE and CI without distributional assumptions. • Common trap — does not add information — if original sample is biased, bootstrap inherits that bias. • Computational cost — needs many iterations (1000–10000 typical).

front: What is the Cramér-Rao lower bound?
back: • Lower bound on the variance of any unbiased estimator of θ. • Var(θ̂) ≥ 1 / I(θ) where I(θ) is the Fisher information. • An estimator achieving this bound is called efficient. • MLE is asymptotically efficient — achieves CRLB as n → ∞. • Tells you the best possible precision any unbiased estimator can achieve.

front: What is a minimum detectable effect (MDE) and how is it used before an experiment?
back: • MDE — smallest true effect the experiment can reliably detect at given power and α. • Computed from — baseline metric variance, sample size, α, desired power. • If business-meaningful effect < MDE → experiment is underpowered before it starts. • Purpose — sanity-check that the experiment is worth running. • Common trap — computing MDE after results arrive is post-hoc rationalization.

front: What is CUPED and what statistical property makes it work?
back: • CUPED — Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data. • Adjusts metric — Y_cuped = Y − θ(X − E[X]) where X is a pre-experiment covariate. • θ = Cov(Y, X) / Var(X) — removes variance explained by pre-existing user differences. • Works because — Y_cuped has same expected value as Y but lower variance. • Variance reduction — typically 20–50% → narrower CIs → smaller sample needed.

front: What is the peeking problem and what is the correct fix?
back: • Peeking — running a significance test repeatedly and stopping when p < α. • Each check is an additional test — family-wise error rate inflates. • 14 daily checks at α=0.05 → actual FPR ≈ 51%, not 5%. • Fix 1 — pre-specify n and evaluate once at experiment end. • Fix 2 — sequential testing (mSPRT, e-values) — provides always-valid p-values under repeated testing.

front: What is a guardrail metric and how does it affect experiment decisions?
back: • Guardrail metric — one where harm is asymmetric — even small negative impact is unacceptable. • Examples — page load time, error rate, unsubscribe rate. • A guardrail violation → experiment held regardless of primary metric result. • Guardrail check — CI for guardrail metric must not include negative effect beyond tolerance. • Common trap — only checking primary metric and shipping experiments that silently degrade latency.

front: What is network effect contamination in A/B testing (SUTVA violation)?
back: • SUTVA — Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption — one unit's outcome unaffected by others' treatment. • Violated when — users interact (social network, marketplace, messaging). • Treatment group users affect control group behavior → both groups contaminated. • How to fix it — cluster-based randomization (randomize at group level, not user level). • Common trap — any social/collaborative product is at risk — often overlooked.

front: What is a novelty effect in experiments and how do you detect it?
back: • Novelty effect — metric improves in week 1 purely because the feature is new, not because it is better. • Decay — improvement diminishes as novelty wears off in weeks 2–3. • Detection — weekly cohort analysis — compare week 1 lift to week 2–3 lift. • If week-1 lift > 2× week-2 lift, flag as potential novelty. • How to fix it — run experiment long enough for novelty to decay before evaluating.

front: What is the difference between a primary metric and a secondary metric in an experiment?
back: • Primary metric — the single metric the experiment is designed to move — drives the ship/hold decision. • Secondary metrics — directional indicators — provide context but do not drive decision alone. • Only primary metric undergoes the pre-specified significance test. • Multiple testing correction applies if multiple metrics are tested for significance simultaneously. • Common trap — deciding which metric is "primary" after seeing results — HARKing.

front: What is an A/A test and why is it run?
back: • A/A test — two identical groups — no treatment difference. • Purpose — validate that randomization is correct and false positive rate matches α. • Expected — ~5% of A/A tests should show p < 0.05 by chance. • If A/A produces consistent significant results: randomization is broken or system bug. • Also used to measure baseline variance for sample size planning.

front: What is stratified randomization and why is it better than pure random assignment?
back: • Stratified — ensure treatment/control groups are balanced on key dimensions (country, platform, user tenure). • Pure random — can produce imbalanced groups by chance, especially with small n. • Imbalanced groups → confounded results — group difference drives metric, not treatment. • Stratification reduces variance in the treatment effect estimate. • Must be pre-specified — post-hoc balancing checks are not the same.

front: What is the difference between within-subject and between-subject experimental design?
back: • Within-subject — same unit receives both treatment and control (crossover design). • Between-subject — different units in treatment vs control. • Within-subject — higher statistical power (removes between-unit variance), but order effects and carryover are risks. • Between-subject — cleaner causal isolation, no carryover, but needs more units. • Most online experiments are between-subject.

front: What is Bonferroni correction and when is it too conservative?
back: • Bonferroni — α_adjusted = α / k for k simultaneous tests. • Controls family-wise error rate (FWER) — probability of any false positive. • Very conservative when k is large: if testing 100 metrics, α per test = 0.0005. • Too conservative when — tests are correlated, or when controlling individual FDR is sufficient. • Alternative — Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) controls FDR — less conservative for large k.

front: What is the difference between statistical significance and practical significance?
back: • Statistical significance — p < α — result is unlikely under null hypothesis. • Practical significance — effect size is large enough to matter for the business. • Large n makes tiny effects statistically significant — a 0.01% conversion lift can have p < 0.001. • Both are necessary before shipping — statistical significance alone is not enough. • Report effect size with CI, not just p-value.

front: What is a holdout group and how is it different from a control group?
back: • Control group — receives no treatment in a specific experiment. • Holdout group — permanently excluded from all experiments — measures long-term baseline. • Holdout enables estimating cumulative experiment impact over time. • Without holdout — experiment effects compound, hard to measure true baseline drift. • Expensive — holdout means withholding potentially good features from those users.

front: What is variance reduction and why does it matter for experiment sensitivity?
back: • Variance reduction — lowering noise in the metric estimate → narrower CIs → same n detects smaller effects. • Methods — CUPED (pre-experiment covariate), stratification, delta method for ratio metrics. • Halving variance → can detect same MDE with half the sample, or detect 1/√2 × MDE with same sample. • Practical impact — faster experiments, smaller required n, more experiments per quarter. • Common trap — using post-experiment data as covariate — this is leakage.

front: What is a ratio metric and what is the delta method?
back: • Ratio metric — Y = A/B where both A and B are random (e.g., revenue per user, CTR). • Naive variance — treating ratio as a single value ignores correlation between A and B. • Delta method — approximates Var(A/B) using first-order Taylor expansion. • Var(A/B) ≈ (1/μ_B)²Var(A) + (μ_A/μ_B²)²Var(B) − 2(μ_A/μ_B³)Cov(A,B). • Common trap — standard t-test on ratio metrics without delta method → incorrect standard errors.

front: What is HARKing and why is it a threat to experiment validity?
back: • HARKing — Hypothesizing After Results are Known. • Example — experiment finishes, you look at 20 metrics, find 2 significant, then write hypothesis around those 2. • Produces inflated false positive rate — post-hoc hypothesis matching is not confirmatory. • How to fix it — pre-register hypothesis, primary metric, and analysis plan before experiment starts. • Common in analytics — "we looked at segments and found that mobile users in India improved significantly".

front: What is a sequential test (mSPRT) and how does it differ from a fixed-horizon test?
back: • Fixed-horizon — sample size decided upfront; test once at the end — valid but inflexible. • Sequential (mSPRT) — test at any time during the experiment — p-values remain valid under repeated testing. • mSPRT uses a mixture sequential probability ratio test — controls Type I error at any stopping point. • E-values — alternative formulation; composable and easier to reason about. • Tradeoff — sequential tests have slightly lower power than fixed-horizon at the predetermined n.

front: What is experiment interaction and how does running simultaneous experiments cause problems?
back: • Interaction — two simultaneous experiments affect the same users and their effects are not independent. • If experiment A increases engagement and experiment B tests a feature that depends on engagement, results are confounded. • How to fix it — experiment isolation via mutual exclusion layers; or test for interaction effects explicitly. • Mutual exclusion reduces available traffic per experiment — tradeoff with speed.

front: What is the difference between intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol analysis?
back: • ITT — analyze all users as assigned, regardless of whether they actually received treatment. • Per-protocol — analyze only users who complied with their assignment. • ITT — conservative, avoids selection bias from non-compliance — preferred for most online experiments. • Per-protocol — can estimate effect among compliers but introduces selection bias. • Common trap — switching to per-protocol when ITT shows no effect to rescue a null result.

front: What is a trigger condition in experimentation and why does it matter for statistical validity?
back: • Trigger condition — rule that determines which users are exposed to the experiment. • Only users who can be meaningfully affected by the treatment should be in the analysis. • Including non-triggered users dilutes the effect — reduces power and distorts estimates. • Common trap — defining trigger condition post-hoc to include/exclude subsets based on results. • Must be pre-specified and applied consistently to treatment and control.

front: What is the fundamental problem of causal inference?
back: • You can never observe both potential outcomes Y(1) and Y(0) for the same unit. • ATE = E[Y(1) − Y(0)] is unobservable at individual level. • Randomization makes E[Y(0). • T=1] = E[Y(0). • T=0] in expectation — identifies ATE. • All causal methods are workarounds for this missing counterfactual problem. • Without identification assumption, no method recovers causal effect.

front: What is selection bias in causal estimation?
back: • Selection bias — units select into treatment non-randomly based on factors related to outcome. • Makes treated and untreated groups systematically different — naive comparison biased. • Example — users who opt into a new feature are already more engaged. • How to fix it — RCT (randomization removes selection bias), or observational methods that model selection. • Common trap — observational data is almost always subject to selection bias.

front: What is the difference between ATE, ATT, and LATE?
back: • ATE — Average Treatment Effect — causal effect averaged over the full population. • ATT — Average Treatment Effect on the Treated — causal effect among those who received treatment. • LATE — Local Average Treatment Effect — effect among compliers (those induced by instrument to switch). • ATT ≠ ATE when treatment effect is heterogeneous and selection is non-random. • LATE is what IV identifies — not always the policy-relevant parameter.

front: What is the difference-in-differences estimator and what does it assume?
back: • DiD — compares change in outcome for treatment group to change in control group over time. • DiD estimate = (treated post − treated pre) − (control post − control pre). • Key assumption — parallel trends — without treatment, both groups would have evolved identically. • Parallel trends is untestable in the post-period; assessed via pre-period trend comparison. • Fails when — confounding trends differ, treatment timing is endogenous.

front: What is an instrumental variable and when is it valid?
back: • IV — variable Z that affects treatment T but affects outcome Y only through T. • Relevance — Z must be correlated with T (testable). • Exclusion restriction — Z affects Y only via T — untestable, requires domain argument. • IV estimate identifies LATE (effect among compliers). • Classic examples — draft lottery for military service, distance to college for education returns.

front: What is a confounder and how does it bias causal estimates?
back: • Confounder — variable that causes both treatment and outcome. • Creates spurious correlation between treatment and outcome in observational data. • Example — healthier people exercise more AND have better outcomes — health status confounds exercise → outcome. • How to fix it — control for confounder in regression, match on it, or use RCT that breaks confounding. • Unobserved confounders cannot be controlled for — requires IV or other design.

front: What is regression discontinuity design (RDD) and what is its key assumption?
back: • RDD — compare outcomes just above and just below a threshold that determines treatment. • Assumes — units just above and just below threshold are similar on all dimensions except treatment. • Sharp RDD — treatment deterministically assigned at threshold. • Fuzzy RDD — treatment probability jumps at threshold — use IV methods. • Validity threats — manipulation of the running variable, other policies changing at the same threshold.

front: What is propensity score matching and what are its limitations?
back: • Propensity score — P(T=1. • X) — probability of treatment given covariates. • Matching — pair treated and control units with similar propensity scores. • Removes selection bias on observed covariates. • Limitation 1 — unobserved confounders not addressed — only controls for what's measured. • Limitation 2 — overlap assumption — must have treated and control units at all propensity score values. • Common trap — large covariate sets → propensity score well-estimated but overlap fails.

front: What is a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) and how is it used in causal reasoning?
back: • DAG — nodes are variables, directed edges are causal relationships, no cycles. • Used to — identify confounders, colliders, and mediators formally. • d-separation — determines which variables are conditionally independent. • Backdoor criterion — which set of variables to condition on to remove confounding. • Common trap — conditioning on a collider opens a spurious association — the collider trap.

front: What is the collider trap in causal inference?
back: • Collider — variable C where both X and Y point into C (X → C ← Y). • Conditioning on C creates a spurious association between X and Y — even if X and Y are independent. • Example — conditioning on hospitalization (collider) can make two unrelated diseases appear negatively correlated. • Common trap — controlling for a variable just because it's correlated with both treatment and outcome. • Need a DAG to determine what to control for — not just correlation.

front: What is synthetic control and when is it used?
back: • Synthetic control — create a weighted combination of control units that matches pre-treatment trend of treated unit. • Used when — only one treated unit (e.g., a policy applied to one country/state). • Weights chosen to minimize pre-period distance between synthetic and actual treated unit. • Validity — requires good pre-period fit and no treatment contamination in control units. • Common trap — over-fitting the pre-period weights → biased post-period counterfactual.

front: What is the backdoor criterion?
back: • Defines which variables to condition on to block all backdoor paths from T to Y. • Backdoor path — any path T ← ... → Y (through a common ancestor — confounder). • Condition on a set S that blocks all backdoor paths without opening new paths (no collider conditioning). • If backdoor criterion is satisfied, regression of Y on T conditioned on S gives unbiased causal effect. • Requires a valid DAG — wrong DAG → wrong conditioning set.

front: What is the exclusion restriction in IV and why is it untestable?
back: • Exclusion restriction — the instrument Z affects outcome Y only through treatment T — no direct effect. • Untestable because — we cannot observe what outcome would be in a world where Z ≠ 0 but T is fixed. • Must be justified with domain knowledge and theory, not data. • If violated — IV estimate is inconsistent — can produce more biased estimate than OLS. • Relevance (first stage) is testable; exclusion is not.

front: What is the difference between mediation and moderation?
back: • Mediation — T affects Y through an intermediate variable M (T → M → Y). • Moderation — the effect of T on Y depends on the level of another variable W (interaction). • Mediation analysis asks — how much of the effect goes through M? (direct vs indirect effect). • Moderation analysis asks — for whom or when is the effect larger or smaller? • Common trap — controlling for a mediator removes part of the causal effect — biases total effect estimate.

front: What is the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA) and when does it fail?
back: • SUTVA — one unit's outcome depends only on its own treatment, not others' treatment. • Required for ATE to be well-defined. • Fails when — network effects, marketplace spillovers, herd behavior, contagion. • Example — vaccination — vaccinating one person reduces others' infection probability (spillover). • How to fix it — cluster randomization, two-sided market designs, or network experiment methods.

front: What is regression to the mean and why is it a causal inference trap?
back: • Extreme values tend to be less extreme on subsequent measurement due to random noise. • Pre-selecting units based on high/low values → post-measurement appears to change, even without intervention. • Example — students who score very low on a test improve on retest — not because of any intervention. • Common trap — observational studies targeting "high-risk" groups will show apparent improvement by regression alone. • How to fix it — control group with same selection criterion but no treatment.

front: What is a JOIN type in SQL and when should you use each?
back: • INNER JOIN — only rows with matching keys in both tables. • LEFT JOIN — all rows from left, NULL for non-matching right — use for optional relationships. • RIGHT JOIN — same as LEFT but reversed — prefer LEFT JOIN for readability. • FULL OUTER JOIN — all rows from both, NULLs where no match. • CROSS JOIN — cartesian product — every combination — use only when intentional; extremely expensive on large tables.

front: What is a window function and when is it used?
back: • Window function — performs calculation across a set of rows related to current row without collapsing them. • Unlike GROUP BY — retains individual rows. • Common — ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), LAG(), LEAD(), SUM() OVER(), AVG() OVER(). • PARTITION BY — defines the group; ORDER BY: defines order within group. • Use — running totals, rankings, lead/lag comparisons, deduplication with ROW_NUMBER().

front: What is a CTE and how does it differ from a subquery?
back: • CTE (WITH clause) — named, reusable query block defined before main query. • Subquery — inline query embedded in FROM or WHERE clause. • CTE — improves readability; can be recursive (for tree/graph traversal); may or may not be materialized (planner-dependent). • Subquery — may be optimized more aggressively by planner (pushed down, collapsed). • Common trap — assuming CTEs are always materialized in Postgres — they are now inlined by default unless marked MATERIALIZED.

front: What is a north star metric and what makes one good vs bad?
back: • North star — single metric that best captures long-term product value delivered to users. • Good — directly tied to user value (not company value), predictive of long-term retention and revenue, actionable by teams. • Bad — vanity metric (pageviews, downloads), easy to game, not causally tied to user value. • Example of good — "weekly active users completing core action" vs bad: "total registered users". • Common trap — optimizing for a metric that diverges from actual user value → Goodhart's Law.

front: What is Goodhart's Law and where does it apply?
back: • Goodhart's Law — when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. • Metric becomes an objective → people optimize the metric directly rather than the underlying construct. • Examples — click-through rate → clickbait; code coverage → trivial tests; session length → addictive dark patterns. • How to fix it — use multiple metrics with guardrails; separate the measurement metric from the optimization target. • Applies everywhere — OKRs, ML model metrics, product analytics, HR evaluations.

front: What is the difference between a leading and lagging indicator?
back: • Lagging — measures outcome after the fact — revenue, churn, NPS. • Leading — measures activity that predicts future outcomes — daily active users, activation rate, feature engagement. • Lagging — accurate but too slow to act on — a revenue drop tells you something already went wrong. • Leading — actionable early but may not perfectly predict outcomes. • Good system — define which leading metrics predict lagging outcomes — with evidence.

front: What is denominator choice and why is it the most important decision in metric design?
back: • Denominator defines the population the metric is computed over. • Wrong denominator — "conversion rate" = orders / users who ordered → always 100%. • Right denominator — orders / users who visited checkout → meaningful rate. • Denominator determines — what question is being answered, who is in scope, what change looks like. • Common trap — using the easiest available count as denominator without questioning what the metric should measure.

front: What is a guardrail metric and what role does it play in product decisions?
back: • Guardrail — metric where any degradation beyond a threshold vetoes the decision, regardless of primary metric. • Examples — page load time (p95 must not increase > 100ms), error rate, unsubscribe rate. • Purpose — prevent optimizing one metric by harming another. • In experiments — guardrail violation → hold/investigate, even if primary metric is positive. • Common trap — only defining guardrails after an incident — design them before experiments run.

front: What is survivorship bias in analytics?
back: • Survivorship bias — analyzing only entities that "survived" a process — ignores dropouts and failures. • Example — measuring average revenue of retained users ignores churned users entirely. • Leads to — overoptimistic estimates, wrong attribution. • Example in ML — training on users who continued to use the product → model never learned patterns of those who left. • How to fix it — include all entities that entered the funnel in the denominator, not just those who completed it.

front: What is the difference between ratio metrics and count metrics in analytics?
back: • Count — absolute number (total purchases, total users) — doesn't normalize for exposure. • Ratio — numerator / denominator (purchase rate, CTR) — normalizes for exposure. • Count metrics — misleading when denominator changes (more users → more events naturally). • Ratio metrics — more interpretable for change analysis. • Common trap — mixing count and ratio metrics in comparisons without normalization — apple-to-orange.

front: What is a Type I vs Type II error in a business decision context?
back: • Type I (false positive) — conclude there is an effect when there isn't — ship a change that doesn't work. • Type II (false negative) — conclude there is no effect when there is — miss a change that would have helped. • Business asymmetry — in most product decisions, Type I costs are low (ship something neutral); in safety/fraud decisions, Type I costs are very high. • Threshold adjustment — lower α (stricter) reduces Type I; higher power reduces Type II. • Design your threshold based on the asymmetric cost, not convention.

front: What is cohort analysis and what insight does it provide that aggregate metrics miss?
back: • Cohort analysis — group users by a common characteristic (signup date, first purchase month) and track behavior over time for each group. • Insight — reveals retention curves, lifetime value patterns, whether product quality is improving. • Aggregate metrics hide — a declining retention rate masked by growing new user acquisitions. • Example — DAU growing but 30-day retention dropping → new users offset by accelerating churn from older cohorts. • Common trap — measuring retention on all users at once mixes cohorts with different histories.

front: What is selection bias in analytics and how does it affect conclusions?
back: • Selection bias — analyzed population is not representative of the target population. • Example — survey sent to existing users → captures only non-churned users → overestimates satisfaction. • Product analytics trap — analyzing only users who completed onboarding → misses those who dropped off. • How to fix it — define population at entry point of the funnel, not completion point. • Applies to — NPS surveys, user interviews, A/B test population selection.

front: What is the difference between output and outcome in product design?
back: • Output — what was built or shipped (feature, page, report) — under the team's control. • Outcome — change in user or business behavior resulting from the output — what actually matters. • Teams often track outputs (features shipped) when they should track outcomes (retention improved). • Product teams should be accountable for outcomes, not just outputs. • Common trap — measuring team success by features shipped — Goodhart's Law applied to product.

front: What is a human-in-the-loop system and when is it necessary?
back: • Human-in-the-loop — humans review, approve, or override automated system decisions at key points. • Necessary when — decisions have high stakes (credit, medical, legal), model confidence is low, errors are hard to reverse, accountability is required by regulation. • Design — surface decision with confidence score and rationale; require override reason; log all decisions. • Common trap — automating fully when humans add genuine value — false efficiency, real accountability gap. • Common trap — requiring human review for every low-stakes decision — bottleneck with no value.

front: What is alert fatigue and how is it addressed in operational systems?
back: • Alert fatigue — so many alerts fire that operators stop trusting or responding to them. • Caused by — low precision (many false positives), insufficient threshold tuning, no severity tiers. • Consequences — real incidents missed, on-call burnout, reactive culture. • How to fix it — track alert precision (what fraction of alerts are real?), tier alerts by severity, reduce noise before adding new alerts. • Rule — every alert should be actionable — if you can't act on it, it shouldn't page.

front: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative user research?
back: • Quantitative — numeric, statistical — surveys, analytics, A/B tests — answers "how many" and "how much". • Qualitative — exploratory, narrative — interviews, usability tests, diary studies — answers "why" and "how". • Quantitative tells you what is happening; qualitative tells you why. • Best practice — use quantitative to find anomalies; qualitative to explain them. • Common trap — building entirely on quantitative data — misses nuanced motivations and unmet needs.

front: What is progressive disclosure in UX and why does it matter for data products?
back: • Progressive disclosure — surface only the information needed at each decision point; reveal more detail on demand. • Reduces cognitive load — users aren't overwhelmed by all possible information at once. • In data products — show summary metric, allow drill-down to segment → root cause → raw data. • Common trap — showing all data by default — users can't find the signal in the noise. • Key design principle — high-level view must be actionable without clicking deeper.

front: What is an SLA, SLO, and SLI in reliability engineering?
back: • SLI (Service Level Indicator): specific metric measuring service behavior (p99 latency, error rate). • SLO (Service Level Objective): target value for an SLI (p99 latency < 200ms, 99.9% availability). • SLA (Service Level Agreement): contractual commitment with consequences for violation. • SLO is internal; SLA is external — SLO should be stricter than SLA to provide buffer. • Common trap — setting SLO = SLA — no buffer means first SLI degradation immediately violates external contract.

front: What is an error budget in reliability engineering?
back: • Error budget — 1 − SLO target — allowed "downtime" or degradation before SLO is violated. • 99.9% SLO = 0.1% error budget = ~8.7 hours per year. • When budget is consumed — freeze feature releases until reliability improves. • When budget is ample — ship faster, take more risks. • Aligns incentives — product and engineering share accountability for reliability vs velocity tradeoff.

front: What is feature flagging and what does it enable?
back: • Feature flag — conditional code path that can be enabled/disabled at runtime without deployment. • Enables — dark launches (deploy code, enable for 0% users), gradual rollout, kill switch for broken features, A/B testing at code level. • Decouples deploy from release — code can be in production but invisible to users. • Common trap — accumulating stale feature flags that are never cleaned up — adds code complexity and tech debt.

front: Pearson correlation — what does it measure, when do you use it, and when does it fail?
back: • Pearson correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship on a unit-free scale from -1 to +1. • It is basically normalized covariance, so you can compare associations across variable pairs even when units differ. • Use it for EDA, collinearity checks, and linear feature screening. • It can be near 0 even when a strong non-linear relationship exists. • It is sensitive to outliers. • Do not interpret r as proportion of variance explained — that is r², not r.

front: Standard deviation — what is it useful for, and what are its limits?
back: • Standard deviation puts variance back in the original units, so spread is easier to interpret next to the mean. • Use it for communicating variability, z-scoring, and confidence intervals like mean ± z·σ/√n. • Bigger SD means the data is more spread out around the mean. • But SD is sensitive to extreme values, so skewed or heavy-tailed data can make it misleading. • Do not treat SD as a “safe range” unless the data is roughly normal.

front: How do you interpret A/B test results before making a launch decision?
back: • 1. First check SRM. If SRM fails, I do not trust the experiment. • 2. Check primary metric lift: absolute and relative. • 3. Check statistical significance with the right test, plus p-value and confidence interval. • 4. Guardrails. • 5. Check key pre-defined segments to see whether the direction is consistent and whether any important segment is meaningfully harmed. • 6. Decide: roll out, ramp, segment-rollout, rollback, or iterate.

front: Interpreting experiment results — what commonly goes wrong?
back: • Do not decide from p-value alone. • Do not ignore guardrail failures because the primary metric looks good. • Do not trust results with SRM or peeking. • Do not assume the average effect applies to every segment. • Do not over-generalize beyond the tested population or time period. • Checkout test: p = 0.03, conversion +1.8%, guardrails clean, SRM clean.

front: What makes a good experiment metric?
back: • 1. Valid = actually measures the outcome the treatment is meant to affect • 2. Sensitive = moves if the treatment truly works • 3. Stable = low enough variance to detect realistic effects • 4. Aligned to business value = improvement should matter to the business • 5. Must be measurable at the randomization unit • 6. Must be measurable within the experiment window

front: What is SRM, and why is it a mandatory experiment check?
back: • SRM means the observed split between control and treatment does not match the intended randomization ratio. • Example: expected 50/50, observed 48/52. • SRM usually means a bug in assignment, logging, filtering, or routing — not a real treatment effect. • It is a pre-analysis validity check: if SRM exists, the experiment result is not trustworthy. • Test was meant to be 50/50, but counts are 48,200 vs 51,800. • SRM check fails. Investigation finds a redirect bug dropping mobile users from treatment.

front: SRM — what do you do if you detect it, and how do you check it?
back: • Do not continue outcome analysis if SRM is present. • Even a small imbalance can mean systematic bias, not random noise. • Check SRM with a chi-square goodness-of-fit test on assignment counts. • Also check it by platform, country, browser, or key segment, because a global pass can hide a segment-level failure. • Typical rule: p • Fix the assignment / logging bug and re-run the experiment.

front: What is the unit of randomization, and how do you choose it?
back: • The unit of randomization is the entity assigned to control or treatment: user, session, device, account, market, etc. • Choose the unit so assignment is stable, users do not see both experiences, and interference is minimized. • In most product tests, randomize at the user level if the user can return multiple times. • Do not randomize at a coarser level than needed, because that usually reduces power. • Feed ranking test: randomize by user, not session, so each user sees one consistent ranking system.

front: What is the alternative hypothesis (H1), and how do you choose one-tailed vs two-tailed?
back: • H1 is the claim you want evidence for if H0 is false — that a real difference or effect exists. • It also determines whether the test is one-tailed or two-tailed. • One-tailed: use only when you care about one direction only and would ignore the other direction. • Two-tailed: safer default when either increase or decrease matters. • Do not switch tails after seeing results — that is p-hacking. • H1 is not the MDE: H1 says an effect exists; MDE says how big an effect the test is powered to detect.

front: Type I vs Type II error — how should you interpret them in practice, and what commonly goes wrong?
back: • Type I = your accepted false positive risk. • Type II = your missed detection risk. • Do not say a non-significant result proves “no effect” — it may just be underpowered. • Correct phrasing: “we did not detect an effect at this sample size / MDE / alpha.” • Do not confuse alpha with the overall chance that a significant result is false — the base rate of true nulls matters. • If most tested ideas truly do nothing, even alpha = 0.05 can still produce many false discoveries among “significant” wins.

front: Outcome window — what is it, and what mistakes break it?
back: • Outcome window is the time period after treatment assignment during which you measure the metric. • Examples: 7-day conversion, 30-day retention. • Define it before the experiment so users get a fair and consistent chance to show the outcome. • Do not extend the window after seeing results — that is p-hacking. • Do not include outcomes that happen before treatment could realistically act. • Do not make the window so short that most users never had a chance to convert.

front: How do sample size and variance affect confidence intervals and MDE?
back: • Statistical precision is driven mainly by sample size n and metric variance σ 2 • SE = σ 2 /n 1/2 • Larger n → smaller standard error → narrower confidence intervals and smaller MDE. • Higher variance → larger standard error → wider confidence intervals and larger MDE. • Doubling nnn does not halve uncertainty. To cut MDE roughly in half, you need about 4x the sample.

front: GROUP BY — what does it do, and when do you use it?
back: • GROUP BY collapses rows with the same key(s) into one row per group. • Then you apply aggregates like COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX per group. • Use it for per-entity summaries: revenue per customer, DAU per day, orders per seller. • SELECT date, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS dau FROM events GROUP BY date • This gives one row per date with daily active users.

front: What does an INNER JOIN do, and when should you use it?
back: • INNER JOIN keeps only rows where the join key matches in both tables. • Use it when you want only matched records. • Good for cases like orders with valid customers or payments with valid transactions. • Join orders to products on product_id. • If an order’s product_id is missing in products, that order is dropped from the result.

front: What does ROW_NUMBER() do, and when do you use it?
back: • ROW_NUMBER() assigns a unique sequential number to each row within a partition, based on the specified order. • Use it to deduplicate, pick the latest / earliest row per entity, or do pagination / top-1 per group. • It is best when you want exactly one row per group after sorting. • Keep the most recent event per user: partition by user_id, order by event_timestamp DESC, then keep rn = 1.

front: LAG vs LEAD — what do they do, when do you use them, and what can go wrong?
back: • LAG(col, k) returns the value from k rows before within the same partition; default k = 1. • LEAD(col, k) returns the value from k rows after within the same partition; default k = 1. • Use them for period-over-period comparisons, state transitions, time-to-next-event, previous vs current status, and next order / next session logic. • Example uses: current revenue vs previous month, next order date, previous order status vs current. • Always use ORDER BY inside the window — otherwise previous/next row is undefined. • They do not fix missing time periods: if a month is missing, LAG gives the previous available row, not necessarily the previous calendar month.

front: Top-N per group — what is it, and how do you do it correctly?
back: • It returns the top N rows within each group without collapsing the result. • Use it for top products per category, latest N events per user, best campaigns per channel. • Usually do it with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC), then filter in an outer query / CTE. • Do not use ROW_NUMBER if ties should all be kept — use RANK or DENSE_RANK instead. • ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) → keep rows where rn <= 2 to get each customer’s latest 2 orders.

front: CTE — what is it, when do you use it, and what is the performance trap?
back: A CTE is a named temporary result set defined with WITH before the main query. Use it to break a complex query into clear logical steps, avoid repeating a long subquery, or write recursive queries. It improves readability, not necessarily performance. In many databases, a normal CTE is not materialized by default and may be re-executed each time it is referenced. If the same expensive CTE is used multiple times, prefer a temp table or a materialized CTE where supported.

front: INNER JOIN — what commonly goes wrong, and how do you check it?
back: Biggest risk: silent row loss when keys do not match. NULL keys do not match other NULLs, so those rows also get dropped. After the join, compare row count before vs after against the driving table. If counts dropped, check whether that was expected or caused by missing / bad keys. Closest alternative: LEFT JOIN when you want to keep all rows from the left table even if no match exists. Concrete rule: Need only matched rows → INNER JOIN Need to preserve all left-table rows → LEFT JOIN

front: INNER JOIN: What does an INNER JOIN do, and when should you use it?
back: INNER JOIN keeps only rows where the join key matches in both tables. Use it when you want only matched records. Good for cases like orders with valid customers or payments with valid transactions. Business example: Join orders to products on product_id. If an order’s product_id is missing in products, that order is dropped from the result.

front: ROW NUMBER: What does ROW_NUMBER() do, and when do you use it?
back: ROW_NUMBER() assigns a unique sequential number to each row within a partition, based on the specified order. Use it to deduplicate, pick the latest / earliest row per entity, or do pagination / top-1 per group. It is best when you want exactly one row per group after sorting. Business example: Keep the most recent event per user: partition by user_id, order by event_timestamp DESC, then keep rn = 1.

front: ROW_NUMBER() — what commonly goes wrong, and what are the alternatives?
back: If the ORDER BY is not unique, tie-breaking is arbitrary / non-deterministic. So for dedup, always add a tiebreaker column if ties are possible. Without PARTITION BY, it ranks the entire dataset as one group. Use RANK() if ties should share rank and gaps are okay. Use DENSE_RANK() if ties should share rank and gaps are not okay. Concrete rule: Need one unique row per group → ROW_NUMBER() Need tied rows to share rank → RANK() / DENSE_RANK()

front: Running totals — what are they, when do you use them, and what commonly goes wrong?
back: A running total is a cumulative sum ordered by a sequence, usually time. In SQL, do it with SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). Use it for cumulative revenue by date, cumulative signups, cumulative spend per user, quota tracking. Use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for strict row-by-row accumulation. Do not use RANGE when the ORDER BY column has duplicate values — it pulls in all ties at once and causes jumps instead of true row-by-row running totals.

front: Business significance vs statistical significance — what is the difference?
back: Statistical significance asks: is the effect unlikely to be zero? Business significance asks: is the effect large enough to matter? A result can be statistically significant but business-trivial if n is huge and the lift is tiny. A result can be business-relevant but not statistically significant if the test is underpowered. Always translate effect size into business units: uplift × traffic × conversion value = impact. Do not treat “non-significant” as “nothing happened” without checking the CI and whether the test could detect the target MDE.

front: How would you defend the cost weights, especially false approval = 5x?
back: Situation/Goal: The exact ratio is an assumption, but the asymmetry is not. Action: I would say false approvals are far costlier because they create credit loss, collections cost, and capital write-off, whereas rejecting a good applicant is lost revenue and more recoverable. So the 5x is a reasonable policy assumption used for the simulation. Result + scope: The mature answer is to defend the direction strongly and the exact number modestly. In production, I would validate the weight with finance and risk stakeholders. Interviewer lens: They want judgment, not fake precision. Contrast: directionally defensible assumption vs pretending the 5x came from empirical finance data Do not say: “The data proved 5x was the exact business cost.”

front: What does the review band achieve operationally?
back: Situation/Goal: Binary cutoff forces automated decisions in the highest-uncertainty zone. Action: Use the 0.08–0.25 band to route borderline applicants to human underwriters. Result + scope: Automation on confident tails, human judgment in the ambiguous middle. Contrast: forced binary decision vs uncertainty-aware routing.

front: What happens operationally to applicants in the review band?
back: Situation/Goal: The review band only makes sense if it maps to a concrete operating action. Action: Applicants in the middle band route to manual underwriting. I also modeled multiple review-capacity scenarios so the policy could be tuned against operational headcount rather than assuming infinite manual review bandwidth. Result + scope: That makes the review band an operations-aware design choice instead of a purely academic threshold gap. Interviewer lens: Can you connect model outputs to human workflow? Contrast: review as real ops constraint vs review as vague buffer zone Do not say: A vague answer that never says who actually reviews the cases.

front: Why not just use the F1-optimal threshold operationally?
back: Situation/Goal: F1 assumes false positives and false negatives matter symmetrically, which is not true in credit underwriting. Action: I treated the 0.18 threshold as the best binary cutoff for an evaluation sweep, then designed a separate cost-weighted policy with approve and reject thresholds plus a review band. Result + scope: That is more operationally faithful because false approvals were penalized 5x harsh rejects, and the review band lets the system handle uncertainty instead of forcing a binary call on every applicant. Interviewer lens: They want to know whether you can separate evaluation convenience from business policy. Contrast: single F1 cutoff vs asymmetric-cost routing Do not say: “F1 was highest, so that’s what I used in production logic.”

front: Why use a three-way policy instead of binary approve/reject?
back: Situation/Goal: Forcing a binary decision in the model’s uncertainty zone is bad risk management. Action: Added a review band between approve and reject so borderline applicants route to manual underwriting instead of being forced into an automated tail decision. Result + scope: The policy captures uncertainty operationally. It is still a notebook simulation, but it is directionally aligned with real decisioning systems where automated tails and manual review are separated. Interviewer lens: Do you understand operations, not just metrics? Contrast: binary cutoff vs approve/review/reject routing Do not say: “I wanted to try something different.”

front: How do you use sample size vs variance in experiment design, and what commonly goes wrong?
back: Use this relationship to decide whether to run longer / get more users or reduce variance with a better metric or CUPED. If variance is much higher than assumed, the test is underpowered and CIs become wider than expected. If observations are clustered / dependent but treated as independent, variance is underestimated and CIs look falsely tight. Don’t pick a metric just because it is easy to measure — pick one that is in the causal path of the intervention. Business example: DAU may have very high variance and need 8 weeks. A lower-variance per-user session metric may cut that to 2 weeks. CUPED is another lever: reduce variance first, instead of only asking for more traffic.

front: Power — what commonly goes wrong?
back: Do not run an underpowered test and then say “there is no effect.” A null result may only mean the test was too weak to detect it. Do not confuse power with confidence level — power is about Type 2 error, not alpha. Power is not a fixed property of a test; it depends on effect size, alpha, variance, and sample size. Do not do post-hoc power analysis on the observed result — it is usually not useful. Concrete rule: If traffic is too low for the MDE you care about, either run longer, reduce variance, or accept a larger MDE.

front: Primary metric — what is it, and what mistakes break an experiment?
back: The primary metric is the pre-specified metric that answers the business question and drives the ship / no-ship decision. It is the metric the experiment is typically powered on, so it also drives sample size. Keep it to one, or at most two, and define it before the experiment starts. Do not declare many co-primary metrics without multiple-comparison correction — that inflates Type I error. Do not switch the primary metric mid-experiment or post-hoc just because another metric turned significant. Business rule: if the primary metric moves in the desired direction at the pre-specified alpha, the test succeeded by design.

front: SRM: What is it, and why is it a mandatory experiment check?
back: SRM means the observed split between control and treatment does not match the intended randomization ratio. Example: expected 50/50, observed 48/52. SRM usually means a bug in assignment, logging, filtering, or routing — not a real treatment effect. It is a pre-analysis validity check: if SRM exists, the experiment result is not trustworthy. Business example: Test was meant to be 50/50, but counts are 48,200 vs 51,800. SRM check fails. Investigation finds a redirect bug dropping mobile users from treatment.

front: Unit of Randomization: How will you evaluate whether the unit of randomisation is correct?
back: Check no unit appears in both arms — for example, the same user ID should not show up in both control and treatment. Check assignment is stable over time — for example, a user assigned to treatment on day 1 should still be in treatment on day 5, not switch arms.

front: Unit of Randomization: What is the unit of randomization, and how do you choose it?
back: The unit of randomization is the entity assigned to control or treatment: user, session, device, account, market, etc. Choose the unit so assignment is stable, users do not see both experiences, and interference is minimized. In most product tests, randomize at the user level if the user can return multiple times. Do not randomize at a coarser level than needed, because that usually reduces power. Business example: Feed ranking test: randomize by user, not session, so each user sees one consistent ranking system.

front: Bayes’ theorem — what does it do, and why does the base rate matter?
back: Bayes’ theorem updates a prior belief with new evidence to get a posterior probability. Formula: P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B). Use it when you know the likelihood and the base rate, and want the actual probability after observing evidence. Common uses: medical testing, fraud detection, spam filtering. Main trap: do not ignore the base rate and do not confuse P(B|A) with P(A|B). Example: even a 99% sensitive fraud test can produce mostly false positives if fraud prevalence is 1 in 10,000.

front: Central Limit Theorem (CLT) — what does it say, and when do you use it?
back: If you draw random samples of size n from a population with finite mean and variance, the distribution of sample means approaches normal as n grows, regardless of the underlying population shape. That is what lets us use t-tests and z-tests on non-normal data. Use it for confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, and standard errors for means. That is why t-tests can still work reasonably well on non-normal data when sample size is large enough.

front: Central Limit Theorem (CLT) — when does it fail or get unreliable?
back: It gets unreliable with small n + heavy skew / heavy tails. It can fail when observations are not independent. It does not fix biased sampling. Do not blindly apply it to dependent data like autocorrelated time series. Extreme cases like Cauchy / infinite-variance distributions break the usual CLT.

front: Covariance — what does it tell you, and when should you not use it?
back: Covariance tells you the direction of the linear relationship between two numeric variables. Positive covariance → they tend to move together; negative covariance → they tend to move oppositely. It is often used as an intermediate quantity in PCA, regression, and portfolio variance, not as a final business-facing metric. Raw magnitude is hard to interpret because it is in the product of the two variables’ units. Do not compare covariance across variable pairs with different scales — use correlation for comparable strength.

front: Null hypothesis (H0) — what is it, and how should you interpret it?
back: H0 is the default assumption the test is designed to challenge. It is usually no effect, no difference, or no change, stated precisely, e.g. μcontrol = μtreatment Every hypothesis test needs an explicit H0 because the p-value is computed under it. Do not say “we accepted H0” — you only failed to reject it. Do not put what you want to prove in H0 — that belongs in H1 / alternative.

front: Statistical Power: What is it, and how do you use it?
back: Power is the probability of detecting a real effect of a given size if that effect truly exists. Power = 1 − beta. If power is 80%, the test has a 20% chance of missing a true effect of the target size. Use power analysis before the experiment to solve for required sample size, given alpha, MDE, and variance. Business example: If you want to detect a 2pp retention lift, power analysis tells you whether your planned traffic is enough or whether the test is too small to answer that question.

front: What does high model variance mean?
back: Model variance means how much predictions change if you retrain on a different sample from the same population. High variance = overfitting: the model is learning noise, so train performance looks good but test performance drops. In logistic regression, this usually shows up with many features, weak regularization, or too little data. Adding more features without control increases variance; more data and regularization reduce it.

front: What is statistical variance, and when do you use it?
back: Statistical variance measures spread around the mean: average squared deviation from the mean. It is mainly used as an input to standard deviation, standard error, ANOVA, and regression. Because it is in squared units, it is usually not reported directly to business stakeholders. It is sensitive to outliers, so for heavy-tailed data it can be misleading or unstable.

front: Z Score Outlier method: What is it, and when does it work?
back: Z-score flags points that are many standard deviations away from the mean: z = (x − mean) / std. Common rule: flag |z| > 3 as an outlier. Use it when the feature is roughly normal and you want a quick univariate outlier check. It works best as a simple EDA method, not as a universal outlier detector. Business example: If age is roughly normal, very high absolute z-scores can flag suspicious ages.

front: Z Test: What is a z-test, when do you use it, and when should you avoid it?
back: A z-test checks whether a mean or proportion difference is statistically significant when variance is known or sample size is large enough for CLT. Common use: large-sample A/B tests on conversion rate or CTR. Use it when observations are IID and sample size is large. Avoid it for small samples with unknown variance — use a t-test instead. Also avoid it when data is clustered / dependent, because variance will be underestimated. Business example: Compare landing-page conversion rates for two variants with 50k users per arm → two-proportion z-test is fine.

front: Alpha (Significance Level) — Core answer vlt_clean_0004
back: The pre-specified maximum acceptable probability of rejecting H0 when it is actually true (Type 1 error rate). It defines the decision threshold: reject H0 if p <= alpha. Standard values are 0.05 (5% false positive rate) and 0.01 (stricter).

front: Alpha (Significance Level) — Failure vlt_clean_0005
back: Don't lower alpha post-hoc because the result is marginal. Don't apply the same alpha to 20 simultaneous tests without correction — with alpha=0.05 and 20 tests, you expect 1 false positive by chance even under all true nulls.

front: Alpha (Significance Level) — Use vlt_clean_0006
back: Set alpha based on the cost of a false positive in the business context. Use 0.05 as default; use 0.01 when launching a wrong feature is costly; consider 0.10 for low-stakes early exploration.

front: Alternative Hypothesis (H1) — Core answer vlt_clean_0007
back: Specifies the effect or difference you are trying to detect — what you expect to be true if H0 is false. H1 determines whether the test is one-tailed (directional: delta > 0) or two-tailed (non-directional: delta ≠ 0).

front: Alternative Hypothesis (H1) — Failure vlt_clean_0008
back: Don't switch from two-tailed to one-tailed after seeing results to halve the p-value — that is p-hacking. Don't confuse H1 with the MDE — H1 says a difference exists, not how large it is.

front: Alternative Hypothesis (H1) — Use vlt_clean_0009
back: Always paired with H0. One-tailed H1 is appropriate when you only care about improvement (e.g., a new feature can only help, never hurt). Two-tailed is the safe default when direction is uncertain.

front: Bayes' Theorem — Core answer vlt_clean_0029
back: Inverts a conditional probability: given P(B|A), base rate P(A), and likelihood P(B), it derives P(A|B). Specifically: P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(A) / P(B). This allows updating a prior belief with new evidence to get a posterior belief.

front: Bayes' Theorem — Failure vlt_clean_0030
back: Don't ignore the base rate — even a test with 99% sensitivity gives mostly false positives if the base rate is 1 in 10,000. Bayes forces you to account for this. Don't assume P(B|A) = P(A|B).

front: Bayes' Theorem — Use vlt_clean_0031
back: When you know the likelihood (test sensitivity/specificity) and the base rate, and need the posterior (actual probability of the condition given the test result). Fraud scoring, spam filtering, A/B decision frameworks, medical testing.

front: Business Significance vs Statistical Significance — Core answer vlt_clean_0040
